title: How many LoRA adapters actually fit on one GPU
question: When one GPU serves many customers' fine-tunes as LoRA adapters on one shared base model, what does each added adapter cost: holding it on the GPU, or serving it in the same [batch](p1:batching) as the others? How many tenants does that leave per GPU, at what price? Measured on Qwen3-4B, one RTX 4090, [vLLM](p1:vllm) 0.27.1.

requirements.text: Split what adapters cost into what registering them costs and what serving many of them in one batch costs, inside the same server start.
requirements.why: Most benchmarking conflates adapters loaded with adapters active together. The design's prior was that mixing adapters in a batch costs more than loading them, and only a split can test it.

requirements.text: Sweep with synthetic adapters only after a pre-registered check shows they serve like real ones.
requirements.why: The sweep needs 64 adapters of one shape for one base model; of 261 public adapters for Qwen3-4B, 7 qualified. Without a check, "those aren't real adapters" stays open.

requirements.text: Fix the knee threshold, the gate's margin and verdict rule, the SLO and the tenant assumptions before the first measured run; later changes are dated [amendments](p2:amendment).
requirements.why: Otherwise the knee, and the tenants per GPU it sets, could be tuned after the data.

requirements.text: Convert the knee into tenants per GPU and cost per tenant per month, beside artifact 4's cost of dedicated and swapped whole models, with every assumption published.
requirements.why: That three-way number is what a team building a per-customer fine-tune product needs; the design calls it the strongest business number in the portfolio.

requirements.text: Hold image, model, GPU, rank, target modules, request shape and memory budget fixed; prime the [compile cache](p1:compile) per slot count and exclude any start that compiled cold.
requirements.why: In artifact 1 a cold compile cut [KV cache](p1:kvcache) capacity by about as much as 16 slots' buffers take here, so one cold start would fake a memory step.

requirements.text: Report medians across server starts with bootstrap [intervals](p2:interval), never means, and re-derive every published number from committed data with no GPU.
requirements.why: Latency is right-skewed, so a mean describes no real start; a number a reader cannot re-derive must be taken on trust.
requirements.unlinked_reason: Met by process: "Analyse, price, publish" re-runs the analysis byte-identically from data/a5 and artifact 4's committed cost file, with no GPU.

concepts.plain: A fine-tune stored as two small matrices added beside each of seven projections in every layer, instead of a whole new model: megabytes, not gigabytes, so one base model can host many. **Rank** (16 here) is the matrices' width. vLLM computes every adapter at the slot's buffer rank, so the work is set by shape, not by the numbers inside.

concepts.term: Registered versus active, and the slot cap
concepts.plain: **Registered**: loaded into one of `max_loras` GPU slots; each slot's weight buffers take [GPU memory](p1:hbm) whether used or not. **Active**: the distinct adapters among requests batched together right now. In vLLM 0.27.1 `max_loras` is also the cap on distinct adapters per batch, so the two are one knob. Here `max_cpu_loras` = `max_loras` = N: every adapter resident, none swapped in.

**Concentrated** regime: all load on one adapter. **Spread**: round-robin over all N. **Heterogeneity cost** at N = spread minus concentrated, in the same start. **Registered-slot cost** = concentrated at N minus concentrated at 1 slot, across starts: what slots cost when one adapter still carries all the load.

Loss per doubling: m(N) = 1 − T(N) / T(N/2), with T the spread regime's throughput. The **knee** is the first N whose point estimate exceeds τ = 10%, fixed in advance; it lies between N/2 and N, because the sweep only doubles. Slots below it set the slot bound on tenants.

**Requests in the system = arrival rate × time each spends there.** At 8 slots, 64 in flight and about 204 completed a second means about 0.31 s each. One tenant at peak, 0.114 requests a second, keeps about 0.036 requests in the system; KV room for 9 long (8,192-token) requests then fits 250 tenants.

Per start: (synthetic − real) / real for TTFT p50 and throughput. **Pass**: the median's 90% interval lies inside ±5% for both. **Resolution check**: the second real phase against the first must also fit ±5%; if not, the gate could not have seen a 5% difference, so the verdict is **inconclusive**, not pass. Resolved but outside: **fail**.

decisions.title: Separate the two counts by traffic, inside one start
decisions.problem: In vLLM 0.27.1 one setting, `max_loras`, is both the number of GPU slots and the cap on distinct adapters per batch, so configuration cannot hold registered fixed while active changes.
options: Sweep registered adapters only, conflating the two counts as most benchmarking does
Hold extra adapters in CPU memory and swap them into slots
Assign requests to adapters at random
Run both regimes in every start: one adapter, then all N round-robin, in a shuffled order
decisions.chosen: Run both regimes in every start: one adapter, then all N round-robin, in a shuffled order
decisions.why: Same slots, memory and start; only how many adapters the batch mixes differs, so spread minus concentrated is a difference inside one start, and start-to-start variation cancels out of it. Swapping is the resident-versus-swapped mode the design put out of scope. Random assignment of 64 requests over 64 adapters reaches about 40.6 distinct on average; round-robin keeps up to min(N, 64) in flight.
decisions.cost: The registered-slot cost compares different starts, against 1 slot. The check that the regimes differed reads vLLM's running-adapters gauge once a second: a sample of scheduler state, not a count per batch. The gauge also adds cost to the spread regime; 24 control starts with it off bound that at +17 tokens/s [−19, +57].
decisions.why_short: vLLM's one knob cannot separate the two counts; traffic can, with slots, memory and the start held fixed.
decisions.cost_short: The slot cost is compared across starts; the manipulation check is a once-a-second sample; the gauge adds a small cost.
decisions.short: Split by traffic, in one start

serves.because: Concentrated and spread differ only in how many adapters are active, so their gap is the cost of mixing, and the concentrated slope is the cost of slots.
Both regimes share one start's slots, memory and compile state, so nothing but the active count changes between them.

uses.because: Because the slot count and the in-batch cap are one knob, the split has to come from traffic.
The two regimes yield the two subtractions.

decisions.title: Report memory as capacity; name the slot cost
decisions.problem: The design claimed the cost was "dominated by batch heterogeneity, not by memory". Reading vLLM's source showed two flaws: at 29-token requests the KV cache can never fill, and the one-adapter regime also pays a kernel cost that grows with slots.
options: Call the one-adapter regime's slowdown memory, as the August design did
Split the slot cost with a `--specialize-active-lora` diagnostic at 1, 16 and 64 slots
Three parts: heterogeneity cost, registered-slot cost, and memory as a capacity ceiling
decisions.chosen: Three parts: heterogeneity cost, registered-slot cost, and memory as a capacity ceiling
decisions.why: 64 requests in flight need about 2,048 tokens of KV against at least 42,864, so the scheduler never waits for memory and its effect on latency is zero by construction. The LoRA kernels launch `max_loras + 1` slices whatever the batch holds (65 at 64 slots, 2 at 1), so the one-adapter slope is named the registered-slot cost, never memory. Memory becomes tenants instead, through Little's law.
decisions.cost: The diagnostic ran out of GPU memory during CUDA-graph capture at 64 slots, at budgets 0.85 and 0.80: it asked for 4.5 times as many graphs. It was cut before the first measured run and H4 withdrawn, so −450 tokens/s stays unsplit between the launch grid, host-side bookkeeping or anything else that scales with slots.
decisions.why_short: KV never fills at this request shape, and the slot cost is kernel overhead, so calling either one memory would mislabel it.
decisions.cost_short: The diagnostic that would split the slot cost ran out of memory and was cut; −450 tokens/s stays unsplit.

serves.because: Each part of the change is named for what causes it, so the split does not credit kernel overhead to memory.

uses.because: The concentrated slope becomes the registered-slot cost, a kernel cost, not a memory one.
KV capacity enters the answer as a bound on tenants, through Little's law.

decisions.title: License synthetic adapters with an equivalence gate
decisions.problem: Public adapters for Qwen3-4B vary in rank, modules and base; the sweep needs 64 of one shape. Weight values should not change serving cost, but saying so invites "those aren't real adapters".
options: Public adapters only, at whatever count qualifies (the design's fallback)
Assert that weight values cannot matter, with no check
Artifact 2's tolerance band from three repeats
A margin taken from per-start spread
4 real vs 4 synthetic in one 8-slot server: the median difference's 90% interval inside ±5%, plus a real-vs-real resolution check
decisions.chosen: 4 real vs 4 synthetic in one 8-slot server: the median difference's 90% interval inside ±5%, plus a real-vs-real resolution check
decisions.why: Cost is set by shape: vLLM computes at the buffer rank, and a dense multiply does the same work for any values. Ignore-EOS (always 16 output tokens) and prefix caching off close the one path from weights to cost, what the model generates. The margin is half the knee threshold, so a passing bias cannot move the knee by itself. Artifact 2's band does not fit one number, and a per-start margin would have made the gate nearly impossible to fail.
decisions.cost: The gate tested one point, 8 slots; the other sweep points rest on the shape argument. It licenses serving cost at rank 16, these seven modules and this base model, nothing about output quality or other ranks. Single-phase TTFT turned out to vary ±10–15% within a start, so the resolution check needed far more starts than planned.
decisions.why_short: Shape sets serving cost, but the claim is checked against real adapters, with a margin tied to the knee and a check that the gate can see 5%.
decisions.cost_short: One point tested; licenses nothing about quality or other ranks; the noisy resolution check needed many more starts.

serves.because: The sweep's synthetic adapters are used only once real ones serve within ±5% of them.
Margin, interval, metrics and verdict rule were committed in the pre-registration, and the runner refuses the campaign until the gate passes.

uses.because: Rank and target modules set the work, which is why random weights can stand in.
The resolution check is what makes "no difference found" mean something.

decisions.title: Inconclusive twice: enlarge, then replace, both disclosed
decisions.problem: The 24-start pilot was inconclusive: phase-to-phase TTFT noise left the resolution check wider than ±5%. The larger rerun lost 52 starts to one bad host and was inconclusive again, by 0.81 points.
options: Apply the design's fallback: public adapters only, a smaller sweep
Change the decision rule
A larger gate of 72 or 108 starts
144 starts in a fresh store (Amendment 1), then replace exactly the 52 lost starts (Amendment 3)
decisions.chosen: 144 starts in a fresh store (Amendment 1), then replace exactly the 52 lost starts (Amendment 3)
decisions.why: The pilot showed noise, not bias: no drift by phase position, real and synthetic phases a few milliseconds apart. Scaling the pilot's interval widths by the square root of the count, 144 scheduled starts (about 139 usable) were estimated to narrow the resolution check enough, with no guarantee; an earlier 72-start sizing had left that check out. The 52 losses died before serving a request (CUDA Error 804, driver 570.195.03), so replacing them restores the size Amendment 1 fixed rather than choosing a new one.
decisions.cost: Both amendments were written after a verdict, in response to it. Amendment 1 had said the gate would not run a third time; Amendment 3 extended the second run instead, decided after seeing the 88-start result. The final TTFT resolution check passes by 0.05 points and sits above zero: the second real phase ran about 2% slower than the first, an order effect not investigated.
decisions.why_short: Both misses were noise and a host fault, not adapter bias; more starts, then exact replacements, restored the size fixed beforehand.
decisions.cost_short: Two data-dependent extensions, disclosed; the final check passes by 0.05 points with an uninvestigated order effect.

serves.because: The synthetic adapters were licensed by a gate that finally could resolve ±5%, not waved through.
Each change is an appended amendment saying what had been seen; nothing above it was edited, and the margin and rule never moved.

uses.because: Both misses were inconclusive verdicts: the resolution check, not the synthetic-vs-real difference, fell outside ±5%.

decisions.title: A knee rule that errs toward fewer tenants
decisions.problem: "How many adapters fit" has no answer until a rule says what counts as capacity, and the design named a threshold but neither the curve nor the rule.
options: August's knee: a stated threshold, with the curve and rule undefined
Require a doubling's interval to clear the threshold
First doubling whose point estimate loses over 10% of spread throughput; tenants = the smallest of three bounds
decisions.chosen: First doubling whose point estimate loses over 10% of spread throughput; tenants = the smallest of three bounds
decisions.why: A loss per doubling is a ratio, so it does not depend on absolute throughput. Requiring the interval to clear 10% would miss a real but noisy drop and push the knee, and tenants, upward; the point-estimate rule errs toward fewer. Tenants = min(slots below the knee, measured throughput ÷ one tenant's peak rate, KV ceiling through Little's law), each input fixed in advance.
decisions.cost: The 8-to-16 doubling loses 10.7% [9.2%, 11.5%]: the point crosses 10%, the interval does not clear it. If that is noise, the slot bound is 16 and cost per tenant halves. And 8 is a lower bound in any case: only the all-resident case was measured.
decisions.why_short: A significance rule would push the knee, and tenants, upward on a noisy drop; the point-estimate rule errs low.
decisions.cost_short: The first crossing, 10.7% [9.2%, 11.5%], is unresolved; if it is noise, tenants double.

serves.because: τ, the curve and the rule were committed before the data, so the headline count could not be chosen afterwards.
The knee sets the slot bound, which here sets tenants per GPU and so the price.

uses.because: The rule is the knee's definition.
The memory bound on tenants comes from Little's law.

decisions.title: Price adapters beside whole models, labelled
decisions.problem: The business answer compares cost per tenant three ways, but artifact 4's dedicated and swapped costs come from its simulator, and artifact 4 moved to Qwen3-1.7B after its Qwen3-4B pair failed a memory check.
options: Publish without artifact 4's costs (the plan stops instead)
Move this artifact to Qwen3-1.7B to match artifact 4
Keep Qwen3-4B; three bars at one rate, labelled not like-for-like and resting on a failed simulator
decisions.chosen: Keep Qwen3-4B; three bars at one rate, labelled not like-for-like and resting on a failed simulator
decisions.why: One shared rate, $1.1095 per GPU-hour (Amendment 2), and code that refuses a table at another rate. What the comparison can carry is the shape of the choice: swapping pays per switch, resident adapters pay per co-active adapter.
decisions.cost: The bars share a unit and a rate and nothing else measured: different model sizes, output lengths and traffic. Artifact 4's simulator failed its gate at exactly this point (10 of 13 bins missed), so the swapped bar's error direction is unknown and the dedicated bar is untested; the adapter bar, set beside them, inherits that.
decisions.why_short: The three-way table is the business answer, so it is shown, at one shared rate, with its limits on its face.
decisions.cost_short: The neighbouring bars come from a simulator that failed validation, on a smaller model: not a like-for-like price list.

serves.because: Tenants become dollars beside the whole-model alternatives, with the rate and every assumption stated.

uses.because: The adapter bar is the GPU's monthly cost divided by the slot bound the knee sets.

results.title: Throughput as adapters are added: one active, or all

chart.note: Whiskers: 95% bootstrap interval of the median across 23 or 24 starts. Single starts scatter more widely than the whiskers.

results.axis: Measured: Qwen3-4B on one RTX 4090, 64 requests in flight, 13 prompt and 16 output tokens. Each point is a median over server starts; both lines come from the same starts.
results.read_as: The gap between the lines at each N is the heterogeneity cost; the top line's own fall is the registered-slot cost. Spread TTFT p95 rose from 108 to 141 ms, far inside the 1 s SLO: all 64 served.
results.takeaway: Holding 64 adapters but using one costs about an eighth of throughput; using all 64 at once costs about half.
results.arithmetic: Concentrated 3,577 → 3,127 tokens/s (−450, 12.6%); spread 3,568 → 1,835, about half. Every point is a median of per-start throughput: successful output tokens over total phase time.

results.title: The knee: throughput lost per doubling of active adapters

chart.note: Whiskers: 95% bootstrap interval of the ratio of medians. A crossing is resolved when the whole whisker clears the line: at 32 and 64, not at 16.

results.axis: Measured: m(N) = 1 − T(N) / T(N/2), with T the spread regime's median throughput (every registered adapter active).
results.read_as: The first point above the line is 16, so the knee lies between 8 and 16 and the slot bound is 8. The point at 16 crosses; its whisker, 9.2 to 11.5, does not clear 10%.
results.takeaway: Past about 8 co-active adapters each doubling costs more than a tenth of the GPU's throughput, by a rule fixed before the data; the first crossing is not resolved.
results.arithmetic: At 16: 1 − 2,911 / 3,260 = 10.7%. Rounded to one decimal, the 2-slot whisker's low end is 0.0 (0.03%).

results.title: At 64 adapters: mixing versus merely holding them

rows.label: Gauge's own share of the first

results.axis: Measured, 95% bootstrap intervals of the median. Heterogeneity: paired within each of 24 starts. Registered-slot: concentrated at 64 slots against at 1 slot, across starts. Gauge: the heterogeneity cost with the gauge on minus 24 control starts with stats logging off.
results.read_as: The two costs' intervals are far apart, so H2 holds: the batch's mix costs more than the slots. The gauge's interval straddles zero: at most about 57 tokens/s of the 1,290.
results.takeaway: What customers' traffic does to the batch costs about three times what holding their adapters costs; at no sweep point is the slot cost over 35% of the mixing cost.
results.arithmetic: 1,290 / 450 = 2.87, the post's 2.9. The slot cost is unsplit: the diagnostic that would separate the launch grid ran out of memory.

results.title: The equivalence gate, three times: could it see 5%?
results.axis: Measured: TTFT p50 relative difference per start, median across usable starts, with the 90% bootstrap interval the rule requires. Synthetic vs real: (synthetic − real) / real. Real vs real, the resolution check: (2nd real phase − 1st) / 1st. 23: the pilot; 88: the 144-start rerun after 52 host failures; 137: after Amendment 3.
results.read_as: The top row is not data: it is the margin. A pass needs both intervals of a run inside it. Synthetic vs real is inside from 88 on. Real vs real reaches +11.7% at 23 and +5.81% at 88 (inconclusive both times), then +4.95% at 137: a pass by 0.05 points, sitting above zero. Throughput passed all three runs.
results.takeaway: Synthetic adapters were never measurably different from real ones; what took 137 starts was a gate able to see a 5% difference at all.
results.arithmetic: 196 scheduled − 55 failed − 4 cold compiles = 137 usable. Margin = τ / 2 = 0.05. Final resolution check: 5 − 4.95 = 0.05 points to spare.

results.title: KV capacity falls with slots, and never binds here

refs.label: 64 requests in flight use about this

chart.note: Every start at a point reported the same value, so there is no interval.

results.axis: Measured: the KV cache size vLLM logs at startup, memory budget 0.80 of the 24 GB card. Each slot's weight buffers take memory the cache would otherwise hold.
results.read_as: About 45% of the cache goes by 64 slots, yet it still holds 1,339 of these short requests against the 64 in flight: memory cannot slow this load. At an 8,192-token context it holds 9 at 8 slots, which gives the memory bound.
results.takeaway: Adapters cost memory, but at this shape memory is capacity, not speed. Tenant bounds at 8 slots: 8 by slots, 250 by memory, 1,784 by throughput; slots bind.
results.arithmetic: 42,864 / 32 (two 16-token blocks per 29-token request) = 1,339. Memory bound = throughput bound × 9 / 64 = 1,784 × 9 / 64 = 250.9, rounded down: 250.

results.title: UNVALIDATED NEIGHBOURS: cost per tenant per month
results.axis: All at $1.1095 per GPU-hour. Dedicated and swapped: artifact 4's simulator, Qwen3-1.7B, bursty regime, s = 1.0, which failed its validation (10 of 13 bins missed). Adapter: this artifact's measurement, Qwen3-4B.
results.read_as: Not like-for-like: different model sizes, output lengths and traffic. The adapter bar is an upper bound because tenants are a lower bound; the swapped bar's error direction is unknown; the dedicated bar was never tested.
results.takeaway: Only the adapter bar is measured here. The comparison shows the shape of the choice, per-switch against per-co-active-adapter, not a price list.
results.arithmetic: $1.1095 × 730 h / 8 tenants = $101.24. If the 8-to-16 crossing were noise: 16 tenants, half that.

interview.pitch30: I measured how many customers' LoRA fine-tunes one GPU can serve on a shared base model, and found the cost is not how many adapters you load but how many share a batch. I split the two by running every server start with the load on one adapter and spread over all of them; at the top of the sweep, mixing cost about three times what holding the adapters did. By a knee rule fixed in advance that gives 8 tenants per GPU, a lower bound. Synthetic adapters were licensed by a pre-registered gate that needed two disclosed extensions before it could pass.
interview.pitch120: Products that give each customer a fine-tune serve them as LoRA adapters on one base model, and people ask how many adapters fit. That mixes two costs: adapters held in GPU slots, and adapters active in the same batch. In vLLM one setting sets both, so I separated them by traffic: every server start ran its load once on a single adapter and once round-robin over all registered ones, so the gap is paired inside the start. I swept 1 to 64 adapters on Qwen3-4B on one RTX 4090, 24 starts per point. The adapters were synthetic, which I only used after a pre-registered equivalence gate against 4 real ones. That gate came back inconclusive twice, once from phase-to-phase noise and once after a bad host killed 52 starts, and I extended it through two post-hoc amendments, disclosed as such, until it passed. At 64 adapters, mixing cost 1,290 tokens a second against 450 for holding the slots. KV capacity fell 45% but never bound at this request shape. By the knee rule, each doubling past 8 co-active adapters costs over a tenth of throughput: 8 tenants per GPU, about $101 a month each as an upper bound. The comparison with whole-model serving leans on artifact 4's simulator, which failed its validation, so I don't present those bars as findings.

followups.q: Why synthetic adapters, and what does that license?
followups.a: There are not 64 public rank-16 adapters on the seven projections for Qwen3-4B: 7 of 261 qualified. Serving cost is set by shape: vLLM computes at the buffer rank, and a dense multiply does the same work for any values. The one path from values to cost, what the model generates, is closed by ignore-EOS and prefix caching off. The gate then checked it at 8 slots. It licenses serving cost at this rank, these modules, this base; nothing about quality or other ranks.

It was data-dependent, and the post says so: I decided it after seeing the 88-start verdict. What bounds it: only the count changed, by exactly the 52 starts a host fault killed before any phase ran, back toward the size Amendment 1 had fixed; the 3 replacements that failed again were counted, not replaced; the margin and rule never moved. Amendment 1 was post-hoc too, and the final resolution check passes by only 0.05 points.

followups.q: Why don't the cost bars count as a finding?
followups.a: Dedicated and swapped come from artifact 4's simulator, which failed its pre-registered validation at exactly this operating point: 10 of 13 bins outside the band of three real repeats, 1 of 2 held-out cells passed. Its swap cost fits no single value, so the swapped bar's error direction is unknown; dedicated was never tested by the gate. The bars also cross model sizes, Qwen3-1.7B against 4B. Only the adapter bar is measured, and it is an upper bound.

Not fully, and the post says so next to the headline. The 8-to-16 doubling loses 10.7%, interval 9.2% to 11.5%: the point crosses 10%, the interval does not clear it. If that is noise the bound is 16 and the cost per tenant halves; the rule was registered to err toward fewer. And 8 is a lower bound anyway: only all-resident adapters were run, while vLLM can hold more in CPU memory and swap them into slots.

followups.q: If memory isn't the cost, why does KV capacity fall 45%?
followups.a: Each slot's weight buffers take memory the KV cache would use: 78,208 tokens at 1 slot, 42,864 at 64. But a request here holds 29 tokens, two 16-token blocks, so 64 in flight use about 2,048; the scheduler never waits for KV. Memory matters as capacity: at an 8,192-token context the cache holds 9 requests at 8 slots, a bound of 250 tenants, and for long contexts it would bind before throughput.

Build the failure-streak stop before the first paid run: without it, one bad host consumed 52 gate starts. Size the gate for its resolution check, not only its main interval: an earlier 72-start sizing left the check out, and the pilot's 24 could not resolve ±5% through phase-to-phase TTFT noise. Then the sequels the post names: rank as a variable, and resident versus swapped adapters, which turns the lower bound on tenants into a measurement.

interview.limits: One base model (Qwen3-4B), one RTX 4090, rank 16 on seven projections, one short request shape (13 prompt + 16 output tokens at 64 in flight), vLLM 0.27.1: the numbers do not transfer; the mechanism may. All adapters resident in GPU slots, so tenants are a lower bound and the adapter cost an upper bound. The registered-slot cost is unsplit (the diagnostic ran out of memory; H4 withdrawn). The gate tested one point (8 slots), was extended twice after its result was seen, and its TTFT resolution check passes by 0.05 points with an uninvestigated order effect. The knee's first crossing is unresolved. The regime check samples the scheduler once a second. All 191 campaign starts ran on one host. The dedicated and swapped costs come from artifact 4's simulator, which failed validation, on a smaller model; the rate is one billing sample.

recall.q: In vLLM 0.27.1, what two things does `max_loras` set, and why does that force two traffic regimes?
recall.a: The number of GPU slots and the cap on distinct adapters per batch. With `max_cpu_loras` = `max_loras` = N, configuration cannot change the active count while holding the registered count, so traffic does: one adapter or all N, in the same start.

recall.q: Why does a batch spanning 64 adapters cost more than one sharing an adapter?
recall.a: Each row needs its own adapter's pair of matrices: the kernel splits the batch, reads 64 sets of weights per projection per step instead of one, and does 64 small multiplications instead of one larger one, at every layer of every decode step. That is how the kernels are organised; the campaign measured the cost's size, not its breakdown.

recall.q: Why does the one-adapter regime slow down too as slots grow, and why is that not memory?
recall.a: The LoRA kernels launch `max_loras + 1` slices whatever the batch holds; empty slots' slices exit early but are launched (65 at 64 slots, 2 at 1). KV never binds at 29-token requests, so memory cannot be it. What else scales with slots is unknown: the diagnostic was cut.

recall.q: Why is the heterogeneity cost paired within a start, and the registered-slot cost not?
recall.a: Both regimes run in every start, so spread minus concentrated is a difference inside one server start and start-to-start variation cancels. The slot cost compares concentrated at N with concentrated at 1 slot, which are different starts.

recall.q: The gate's real-vs-real check fits inside ±5% but synthetic vs real does not. What is the verdict, and what happens?
recall.a: Fail: the gate could resolve 5% and found a difference. That would be a publishable finding, and the design's fallback applies: public adapters only, at the count that qualifies, with a smaller sweep.

recall.q: Why can random weights stand in for trained adapters, and which two settings close the remaining gap?
recall.a: The work is set by shape (rank at the buffer rank, the seven projections), and a dense multiply costs the same for any values. Ignore-EOS fixes every output at 16 tokens and prefix caching is off, so weights cannot change what is generated or what is cached.

recall.q: Had the knee rule required the interval to clear 10%, where would the knee be, and why was that rule rejected?
recall.a: Between 16 and 32, so 16 tenants: the 32 crossing is resolved, the 16 one is not. Rejected because it misses a real but noisy drop and pushes the knee, and tenants, upward; the point-estimate rule errs toward fewer.

recall.q: How does Little's law turn KV capacity into a bound on tenants?
recall.a: Requests in the system = rate × time. 64 in flight at about 204 completed a second is about 0.31 s each; a tenant at peak (0.114 a second) keeps about 0.036 in the system; room for 9 long requests at 8 slots ÷ 0.036 = 250 tenants.

recall.q: Which requirement does each gate amendment protect, and what do the amendments cost the claim?
recall.a: R2: synthetic adapters are licensed only by a gate that can resolve ±5%. R3: each change is appended and dated, margin and rule unchanged. Cost: both were decided after a verdict, so they are data-dependent and disclosed as post-hoc.
